Yeah, it varies.
Some guys sound like they play.

They cannot play the same thing over and over and make the same variations, over again. They forget the same thing over again. That's quite natural to be written well and you have to follow it. Well I've seen some time in reading in the solo for the trumpet, I wouldn't put that song, I'd put my own in. You know what I mean?
Take it off the music. Even with the score you get off it? Yeah, get off it.

Get off it, oh yeah. Don't sound right to me like it's a score, you know? My imagination, that's what it is, you know? And if it doesn't sound better, well I'd put it in there than it's on the paper, time. And to me it does. That's how those things get in there. Yeah, you get a piece of music wrote and a trumpet solo and you don't like it, put another one in there. A couple of bars, or a different break or something like that, or your own.
One thing I never could understand, how does a band get organized on something like that? How do you know who's going to play the lead?

Oh well that's in front. See like mostly a man says he's got his job and other boys, well he tends to probably the money proposition, the money part of it, but mostly the trumpet player will lead that band. Now if they figured sax is a stronger man in other words, you know, I'd let him lead the band, follow him. Follow him. But mostly between the trumpets and the sax, you know. And they used to be clarinet before, clarinet and trumpet. They would do the most leading instruments.
Well who did the lead on clarinet in the old days?
Oh like all the more fellas like we mentioned there in Piku. He would play the lead?
He would play the lead, so?

Oh yes indeed, the lead band was sure. He had a lot of work in it, because Piku would run his band and let it live where he wanted, you know. Fragile music like he wanted. Cut it up whatever he wanted to do. He had that part to do.

Now when you started out, say they'd have a six piece band, I'll just choose for example, trumpet, clarinet, trombone, and a bass, and a guitar, and drums. Now, how would you play a tune in those days? Would it be the full band at first, or would it be one man, or how would you start off?
Oh no, we'd all start off together. We'd give the name of the piece quite nicely, most every man member of the band knew the number, melody anyway.
Yeah.

See they knew the melody, and whoever would lead the band was the trumpet player, he knocked off two beats. The band started all in one. Well name the key, you see, because the trumpet key, each instrument plays a different key. If a piano is in E flat, the trumpet would be saying B flat, each man knows his key. Well in other words, you make a variation in that key on the trumpet, they know what key you're in. Each one knows what key he is to play to correspond with the trumpet. That's the way that's done. Then two licks, you have to call it a number, and he'll lead off. That's what he's going to go right on the playing and then he'll right in there with him.
That's the way that's done. How many choruses would the trumpet stay up?

Well sometimes, he'd stay up one, some would take two, all depends on how strong the man was. Sometimes he'd play all through the pieces, three choruses or four choruses, whatever he would play. Most of the time they played three choruses.
In those days?

They'd pick up, yeah, and then he'd rest his lip while the sax or the claret, who they featured in there, and then they'd come in on the last, sometimes the last half of the chorus or the last chorus, all depending on his lips. And some would stay up from the time they knock off till they knock out the band, play all the way through. But you feature one man sometime in a band at a time, whoever you want to take that chorus, that middle chorus. Or if there's five you want to play everybody take a heart, because they say take a heart, each man take a chorus, and the last chorus would go out. But the trumpet player would stay down mostly.
He's a full of a run-potato, that's all he is.
The trumpet player would stay down and rest his lip.
Well did they often take a heart in those days, as much as they do now? Not so much, no, no.

Not today there's a whole lot of solo and stuff like that. Some trumpet players picked up and put that horn out there left until the piece was ended. But if they played nine chords, no way to speak, he'd stay up. Strong though, you know, had to be. Now they'd just take down, wipe your lip, pick up again, get out for a few more hours and ride on again, continue.
But when the clarinet player would be up there?
Well then you could take down, or otherwise play variations with that clarinet.
Would the trombone be playing at the same time? At the same time, yeah, yeah, yeah.

In other words he'd be tearing paper just making those long notes, you know, we call that tearing paper, you know. Ta, ta. They'd take those hearts like they take today now. And the trombone players play almost like a trumpet player today, make all those variations today, you know. At that time they didn't. Just a long slide note, you know, filling in. That's what it was. Very few trombone players take a solo at the time, but most of the time all during the pieces fill in that part, you know. Fill in these parts. It's a lot. It was to blend with the rest of the music, blend together.
Who did they have that could take a solo on trombone good in those days? Huh?
They told me there's so many, they all thought they were good, you know. And did they take many of them?
Who would feature himself much on trombone? A lot of old men, I just can't call names.
What about Frankie Dooson, would he? Or would he play mostly in the ensemble? Frankie, Frankie.
You don't remember Frankie? No, I'm trying to think now. You called him Frankie Dooson. Not Frank, Frank.
We knew what he was in the name. I'm talking about.
Willie Cornish, did you know him? Cornish, Cornish, yeah. Big Cornish.
Yeah, yeah. Did he take many solos? Yeah, most all of them take me solo. They were now.
Oh yeah. In the old days.
In other words, every time. You know what we call it, every time. Each man had to hold that chair.
It wasn't that rattle but guy him about it or whatever he called it.

Kid him about it. Until he wasn't learn to play something. Yeah. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. That was the time. you know, till you wouldn't know, and play something. Well you know, when I went up to

Tyler's Beer Garden, when I first came to town, they had the Avery Tillman orchestra, they were Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman and Dude. Joe Avery, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. And all that time that I'd hear them, the trumpet would play that lead and Avery would be popping away there, you know. Oh, yeah, he was strong for Tillman. Yeah, and then Dude would take down, you know,
take the trumpet down. And Tillman would play the lead. He'd play a lead all the way,

most of the time. Yeah. Right with the trumpet. Well, Tillman would take the lead part of the time. Part of the time, man. And then Joe would accompany him, but there would never be a real solo, there was just a trumpet would take down would be all. No, no, and he'd play right on through. Were there many bands like that in the old days? No, they worked that way too. They worked that way too, in addition to having the solos. Played right on through. And you say there are less solos then and now.

Oh yeah. We were a little hotch then at that time, you know, like too much. Most of the hotch like banjo would take it, a little peak in now and then, you know. Pick a half chorus or a chorus. Today he's instant now. Everybody takes it out of the way, rigged up, and each band, well organized band, take a half a solo, three, four bars solo. Only the other one take down, he'd pick up the solo. That's the way it's written mostly written today, you know. Three, four bars solo. One fella play three bars and the other fella play the other three, all like that. One play four and the other play the other four, all like that. Playing hard to take a whole chorus now. But this fella stand up sometimes, felt good and take two, three choruses, you know. They got tied. That's what Ed White did.
What about Chris Kelly? Who did he have in his band? Do you remember any of those fellas at all?

No. Chris had so many of them. What about Guy Kelly? Do you remember any of the fellas? I did. His brother, well he worked with Papa Celestine a lot. He was, in other words, played second with Papa Celestine most of the time. What did you say about his brother?
Chris? Yeah. Didn't you say something about brother and Guy there?

Oh, they were two brothers, yeah, quite natural. But Guy Kelly, yeah, oh yeah, they were brothers. But Guy Kelly was more musical, you know, reading man. Read more. That's how he stayed more with Papa Celestine. But Chris was just actually anywhere, any little job, three pieces, four pieces, he would get to play it. But they claim he knew a lot of music. He never played it though. I was told he read red, red, yeah, red, nice. He got out of the story. What about this fella, Rochon, you mentioned
the other day? Alexis. Is that his name, Alexis Rochon? Alexis Rochon. And what instrument did he play?
Sax. He was a good man on the sax. And who was this guy, Wright, that played tenor sax? He was a couple by Tredd, he played tenor sax or something. What was it coming in?
Remember his first name? Maybe Alba.

Maybe Alba, huh? You're not sure. I'm not sure. I'm going to it with Alba doing. I think so. I know he's becoming here. We were talking about him this morning, wasn't it? The other day, Rochon. The other day. We were talking about Rochon. Rochon, he's a preacher now, he's out of it too.
I was going to ask you about your education. Did you have any music in school at all?

No, no, no, no, no. It started, I had a niece, cousin rather, on the road years ago. I was around about fifteen. With a regular, a minister or a troop, whatever they call it, traveling around, you know. And she played trumpet. In other words, taking sick or what, she sent the trumpet to her sister, which is Nelisco, today her name is Nelisco Briscoe. And she began to learn on the trumpet. The sister did a twentieth century, it was called a twentieth century trumpet. It was a brass instrument, cornet. On it. And in other words, she gave me, got this guts and she gave me the horn and I picked up the horn and started to play and you know, practicing, you know, by here, by here, by here. And then I went to lessons. What I call it, I told you, Charlo, Charlo Nee at the time. He was a letter carrier and a music teacher at the time. And that's how I started my music.
What was your cousin's name that had a trumpet on the road?
Ran. Ran. We used to call her Ran. Ran Briscoe.
Ran Briscoe.

Well they were years back, yeah. You know some girl troupe. Then when she sent her sister to horn, her sister learned enough to play to join Sweetheart's Rhythm. That was a colored girl band we had here too. They done well and they broke up years back too. The sister learned to dance from her. That's Naliska. That's Naliska. She don't play anymore. Give it up. California, so where I know. They had Sweetheart's Rhythm. It was a known band here at one time. You know, colored man. Girl band. One time.
Were they mostly girls from here?
All girls from here, yeah. Mostly from here.
Do you remember the names of any of those?
No, I wasn't sure.
You better chip that noise.
I got the trumpet from her and that's how I started.
And who was it?
That's the way we're third handed when I got it.
And what minstrel shows did your cousins play with?
Oh I couldn't even tell you that.
You don't know anything about that?
I went on the road most of the time and I didn't know anything too much about no music and shows and stuff at the time, you know.
And your cousin Rand was from here too or not?
Yeah, she was from here. Oh yeah. She had left here as a kid I guess, you know, left home.
You don't hear of many women trumpet players now. No. No. I sure don't. They had one in Chicago.
Sometime I heard a big band on the radio, oh, been a good while back. Not from here though, I know they're not from here. There's some nice, nice music.
I wondered when you were with Celestan. Do you remember what band you were with before you went with Celestan? Or were you Spartan or what?
Mostly Spartan like that, when you get together.
Let's see, that would be, was that before Depression or after or what?
Oh, maybe way before Depression, I imagine.
Way before Depression when you were with Celestan. Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Was it before you were with Paul Barnes?

Yeah, with Celestan, yeah, I imagine so, yeah, yeah. And I joined Paul after. I saw him the other day. Paul? Yeah, they won a, what was that Billy? They played? We met Paul. I was with you. Oh, that's right you were, that's right you were, yeah, yeah.
It was a Sunday after Depression.
I hadn't seen him in a long time. Yeah, you remember when I was?
Yeah, we had a good time. I wanted to see him, yeah, yeah, I enjoyed it. I enjoyed it.
I was really there. He was supposed to visit me out of the way. He came here, yeah. Oh, my old buddy.
You talked about the second line, remember?
Mm-hmm, yeah, yeah, yeah.
I was describing it to you. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. The way it used to be.
Well, you see.
How did the second line act when you were playing with those brass bands?
Well, it was the same thing. I don't think I had no chance.
I imagine they do the same thing.
People were more wasted then.
You think so? People were more wasted then, but now they didn't come down.
You know, the grand marshal used to trick them and all like that.
Oh, that's true. I don't know if they'd do that yet. See the grand marshal was parading and he'd get you to the corner like that.
I think they got nine.
Yeah, they was wasting years now.
Dick Allen?
Mm-hmm.
The parade would be going, the grand marshal would be in lead, you know?
Yeah.

And the band behind quite nicely in the regular line up. And the second line would be on one side of the bank and on the other, you know? My grand marshal would stand in the middle street and it'd make like he was going to turn this way. Yeah. Now you see, now if the second line was on that side of the bank, they'd all rush to get on that side to turn that way. Then he'd turn this way all of them. You see? He'd have all of them. He'd be fun at that time, you know? Oh, the second line would be a dog out. He'd run into each other. Yeah. Yeah. He'd make a motion like he's turning this way to turn the corner that way. And all the second line, I'd run ahead, you know? He'd cross on that side of the bank and he'd just turn around and lead the band this way. That's what's up. The car was going in a way. That's what we used to do it.
Well how did they get around? Did they always walk or did they ride bicycles? Walk, walk, walk.
No, no, walk, walk, walk, walk. On the feet.
I see them riding, let's see, the day I saw them on bicycles, roller skates. Everything, everything.
No, no, no. Now I guess today they do it. They do it. I'm walking. They're walking. Women like them in too.
Oh yes.
Dancing in the streets. Oh, same. Oh, same.
Oh, there'll be some time in the day. I saw when she was really shaking today. Oh man. Old woman about 70 years old and she was out there shaking just like she was a kid again.

Well, I'll tell you Dick something that happened to me. Billy and I. Billy had made a spell of sickness. I knew Billy was sick and I knew it wasn't our habits of falling, making second line. And I was playing somewhere in town, I'll just forget the job we had. I was on the street and one of the boys in the band, John Cashmore, I worked with him a lot, playing that play.
Who do you?

And he told me, look on the back, look who Billy liked that. I said, I know that ain't Billy on the back. And my goodness, I'll tell you the truth, if that wasn't Billy in a way, I'll eat my hat. It ain't no joke. Who could be Billy's twin? I got out the line and run the door and grab her, you know. And the woman faced me and I saw it with me and I suppose she had a boy in front of something in the line like this fella there believing in the dice, I would have got hurt. Yeah. You know, and I come back there and I'll tell you the truth, I'll cut the ball out. It wasn't their fault. I thought, sure. I said, well, Billy, I left Billy home sick and Billy wouldn't follow no parade. I know that wasn't our habits, really, you know. But when you see something with your own eyes, you know what I mean? I felt funny about it. It's the one with that shagging down to the bricks. I gave you. I gave you. That one was shaking on the back. I said, hold my arm, John. So I went to grab it. When I went to grab it, the woman turned her on in the face and it wasn't Billy. I could have got cut, you know. Those fellas, you know, go pull on your girlfriend and things like that. They put a knife on you, you know. And I fell out. I come back and cut them all out. But John was the girl and said, well, look, that's Billy. I said, no, man. Come here, look. And from a distance, I could see. That was Billy to me. I told him I got up on the woman. You know, it was something. He laughed about it.
I saw John today on the bus. He got on the bus.
Who did you know?
John Casimir. John Casimir. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. I told him I'm coming down to the street. Yeah.
My old friend. In fact, I mean all the boys.
Who worked with you when you were in John's band?
Wee. It's been hard to mention all the folks. Who cares? Nine pieces sometimes, you know, on the street. I lived there, but there were so many. I don't know.
You know myself who was John's band? I don't forget them all. I'm trying to remember.
I remember Red on the base. I don't know what become here. Who's Big Red? I always call him Big Red. I don't know. I always call him Red. All I know is the big red skin.
Not Red Claw.
Big man.
Yeah. What does he work with? He had worked with John. No, but I mean does he work for Western Union or somewhere? Do you know?

I don't know what he's doing now. I don't know what he's doing now. I know he did other work, you know, side-lockers. He played most of the music. You know, most of the side-lockers. He wasn't regular enough. He had some other regular work. I don't know what kind of working boys are there.
I wanted to ask you, who were some of your favorite trombone players from the old days?
Well, like I said, Sonny, I remember how he was. I remember the brothers, several of them, before my time.
Sonny Henry?
Petit, yes. I like his playing. Who? Showboy.
Which Petit is that?
I forget his name, old man Petit. He played a bit.
Is that Buddy's stepfather or uncle or something? Stepfather or uncle or something.
Something else in relation. That's Joe Petit. That's Joe Petit. That's Joe Petit, yeah.
And Showboy is worthy of Thomas. Yeah, that's his real name. Oh, yeah.
Well, Showboy, we call him Showboy.
What about clarinet players in those days?
Well, Louie, big guy Louie.
Uh huh.
Piku and all of them like that. Oh, this boy I just mentioned, Cashman, John.
Uh huh.
Awesome. What's this little boy had down there a lot of years ago?
What did you call him?
Melvin.
Melvin Frank.
Melvin Frank. He died. He lived there. He lived there. There were so many of them.
Yeah, let's see now.
I had to get them boys together.
Yeah. Do you have any favorite piano players?
Well, I did work a lot with Kid. You know, with I know this, uh, Brennel. Brennel Sonniac? Oh, yeah. He worked with the past few years. That's how we used to put him on the stool.
Did he have any brothers? Yeah. Who's his brother?
There's one which is called Black, uh, what's his name?
Well that's Lester Sonniac. That's Lester.
That's brother, and then he has another one. I'm going to take a look. Huh?
I'm going to wipe out a choice. I'm going to wipe out a choice. Huh? I'm going to wipe out a choice. I'm going to take a look. Lester?
No, Black. Black is Lester. Now there's another one too there.
And he played piano?
He died and there's two dead that I know of too.
Burnell Sonniac. All of them played, but I mean they never played much out.
Black and Burnell, the only two once they played out. And the girls too. In fact the whole family. They were just like the village people. All the sisters played, sisters, brothers, they all played.
I mean, they played jobs out.
Jobs was only Lester and Burnell. Burnell mostly played out. You know, jobs.
I'm afraid I better turn it off if we're going to get to Sonny's wake. So thank you a million today. Let me get this thing put up. Thanks for you. Okay. .

segments.title: Opening, date, location and names of those present
segments.summary: Recording set-up at De De Pierce's home on 10 January 1960; full names of those present are given.

segments.title: Creole names for musical instruments
segments.summary: Allen asks what trumpet, trombone, banjo, guitar, clarinet, sax, piano, drums, bass and violin are called in Creole; most are the same as English or French.

segments.title: Creole word list: furniture, body, nature and everyday words
segments.summary: Pearsall takes De De through words for objects, body parts, verbs and animals, each repeated three times for the recording.

segments.title: How De De learned French and Creole; the Creole jargon
segments.summary: De De says his mother learned French at the convent and he learned Creole and a broken-up jargon from his family; it is now spoken by few.

segments.title: More words and phrases: going to town, rain, sun, hot
segments.summary: Pearsall and Allen ask for further Creole words and sentences such as 'I am going to town' and 'it is going to rain'.

segments.title: Lyrics of 'A La Ba', first verse: the hog and hot sausage
segments.summary: De De translates the opening verse word by word: going to market for a hog, none to be had, hot sausage instead.

segments.title: 'A La Ba' verse: my dear cousin and your kitchen
segments.summary: De De gives and explains a verse about eating well and drinking wine for free at a cousin's kitchen, and says he sometimes makes up verses as he sings.

segments.title: Verse about the red fish cobayon, and the rice cake calla
segments.summary: De De translates a verse about his mother saying the stewed fish was not good for him, then explains calla, a rice cake.

segments.title: Creole verbs and times of day: sleep, get up, French, morning
segments.summary: Allen asks for verbs and words like couche, arrive, Francais, Creole and matin.

segments.title: The word for brass band and orchestra
segments.summary: De De only knows 'band'; he says in the old days there was no orchestra, brass bands played dance music.

segments.title: Arnold DePass's band: Picklehead Marrero and the trombonists
segments.summary: De De recalls trombone and banjo men in Arnold DePass's band, including Marrero nicknamed Picklehead, and Sonny Henry who sent men out to jobs.

segments.title: How De De improvises variations and departs from written parts
segments.summary: De De says variations just come while playing, and that he swaps out written trumpet solos for his own.

segments.title: Who leads a band: trumpet, sax or clarinet, and Picou
segments.summary: De De explains the leader is usually trumpet, sometimes sax, and earlier clarinet, citing Picou.

segments.title: How a six-piece band started a tune and how choruses were shared
segments.summary: De De describes the band starting together, the trumpet's two-beat lead-in, keys, and trumpet resting his lip while others take choruses.

segments.title: Role of the trombone and old-time trombone soloists
segments.summary: Trombone 'tore paper' with long slide notes in the old days; Willie Cornish is named as someone who took many solos.

segments.title: Avery and Tillman at Tyler's Beer Garden and solos then and now
segments.summary: Allen recalls Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman's band playing lead right through; De De says short solos are the written norm today.

segments.title: Chris and Guy Kelly, Alexis Rochon and a tenor player
segments.summary: De De compares the Kelly brothers, Chris the any-job player and Guy the reader with Celestin, then names sax player Alexis Rochon.

segments.title: Starting on trumpet: cousin Ran Briscoe's horn and early lessons
segments.summary: De De got his first trumpet at about fifteen from a cousin on the road via her sister, then took lessons; the sister later played in Sweetheart's Rhythm girl band.

segments.title: Order of De De's bands: Celestin, then Paul Barnes
segments.summary: De De places his time with Celestin well before the Depression and his joining Paul Barnes after; they recall meeting Barnes recently.

segments.title: Second line and the grand marshal's tricks with brass bands
segments.summary: De De describes how the grand marshal faked turns to fool the second line, which walked and danced.

segments.title: Mistaking a second-line dancer for his wife Billie
segments.summary: De De tells of John Casimir pointing out a woman who looked like Billie, who was home sick, and nearly getting in a fight.

segments.title: John Casimir's band and its players
segments.summary: Allen mentions seeing John Casimir; De De struggles to name his bandmates, recalling a bass player called Big Red.

segments.title: Favorite old trombone players: Sonny Henry, Joe Petit, Showboy
segments.summary: De De names trombonists he liked, including the Petit brothers and Showboy Thomas.

segments.title: Clarinet players of the old days
segments.summary: De De names Big Eye Louis, Picou, John Casimir and Melvin Frank among clarinetists.

segments.title: Piano players: the Santiago family
segments.summary: De De recalls working with Burnell Santiago and his brother Lester 'Black', a musical family of which only those two played jobs.

segments.title: Closing, thanks and heading to Sonny's wake
segments.summary: Allen ends the recording and thanks De De.
